title: Partition, Order, Frame: The Mental Model
objective: After this lesson you will be able to decompose any OVER clause into partition, ordering, and frame; predict exactly which rows each function sees; and explain the evaluation pipeline that makes windows legal where GROUP BY fails.
why: The Advanced primer taught window shapes; this course teaches window *thinking*. Every subtle bug in window SQL — the running total that isn't, the rank that shifts, the LAG that looks at the wrong row — traces to a fuzzy model of partition/order/frame. Seniors debug windows by reciting these three components cold, and this lesson makes them unforgettable.

blocks.text: OVER has three dials, not one

Every window call is `FUNCTION(...) OVER (PARTITION BY … ORDER BY … FRAME …)`. **PARTITION BY** slices rows into peer groups (omit it: one global group). **ORDER BY** sequences rows *within* each partition — and silently changes default frames (the course's biggest gotcha, below). **FRAME** bounds which peers count (default: whole partition without ORDER BY, growing prefix with it). Three dials, each with a default you must know, not guess.

blocks.code:
-- Same function, three dial configurations, three meanings (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
-- Global total on every row (no partition, no order: whole table is the peer set)
-- SUM(hours_studied) OVER ()
-- Per-role total on every row (partition slices, no order: whole slice counts)
-- SUM(hours_studied) OVER (PARTITION BY role)
-- Running total within role (order switches the default frame to growing!)
-- SUM(hours_studied) OVER (PARTITION BY role ORDER BY hours_studied)
blocks.caption: Three OVER shapes: global, partitioned, running — dials decide, not the function

blocks.text: Logical evaluation order: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → **windows** → SELECT → DISTINCT → ORDER BY → LIMIT. Two consequences seniors exploit daily. **Windows see grouped/aggregated results** — you can window over GROUP BY output (rank the per-role averages directly). And **windows can't appear in WHERE** (they don't exist yet) — filter ranks outside via subquery, exactly as the primer taught.

blocks.code:
-- Window over grouped output: rank the role averages (real SQLite/PostgreSQL)
SELECT role, avg_hours,
  RANK() OVER (ORDER BY avg_hours DESC) AS rnk
FROM (
  SELECT role, AVG(hours_studied) AS avg_hours
  FROM developers GROUP BY role
) AS per_role;
blocks.caption: GROUP BY first, windows second — pipeline order as a feature

blocks.text: No frame specified? The default depends on ORDER BY's presence: **no ORDER BY → whole partition** (`RANGE BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW` over unordered peers = everything); **ORDER BY present → growing prefix** (`… CURRENT ROW`) = running computation. Same function text, different peer sets. The professional rule from here on: *always write the frame explicitly* — three extra words that delete a whole bug class.

rows: OVER (PARTITION BY r ORDER BY x)

blocks.title: The ORDER BY you added for display
blocks.text: Adding ORDER BY inside OVER 'just to sort the output' silently converts whole-partition aggregates into running ones — the most common window surprise in code review. Output sorting belongs in the query's own ORDER BY; OVER's ORDER BY defines peer sequence for ranking and frames. Two different jobs, two different clauses.

blocks.query: SELECT role, COUNT(*) AS devs, AVG(hours_studied) AS avg_hours FROM developers GROUP BY role ORDER BY avg_hours DESC;
blocks.note: Run this grouped baseline in the sandbox — it is the inner query of the rank-the-averages pattern above. The window version (real SQLite/PostgreSQL) ranks exactly these four rows: verify the baseline first, then predict each rank before running the full query.

items: OVER = PARTITION (peer slices) + ORDER (sequence, changes defaults!) + FRAME (which peers count)
Pipeline: windows evaluate after GROUP BY/HAVING, before SELECT/DISTINCT/ORDER BY — hence rank-inside/filter-outside
No ORDER BY → whole-partition default; ORDER BY → growing-prefix default — always write frames explicitly
OVER's ORDER BY sequences peers; the query's ORDER BY presents output — never confuse the two

exercise.prompt: (a) In the sandbox, run the per-role GROUP BY baseline and record the four averages in order. (b) In real SQLite/PostgreSQL, write the ranked version (RANK() OVER (ORDER BY avg_hours DESC) on the grouped subquery) plus a running-total version (SUM(avg_hours) OVER (ORDER BY avg_hours DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW)). (c) State in one sentence what changes if you delete the frame clause from (b)'s running total.
hints: Baseline gives four rows (frontend/backend/fullstack/devops averages) — the window queries consume exactly these rows. Predict ranks from the baseline before running.
Ranked version wraps the GROUP BY in a subquery (windows can't rank ungrouped rows into per-role ranks). Running version adds the explicit frame — compare with the frameless twin.
Deleting the frame changes nothing here (ORDER BY present → growing prefix is already the default) — which is precisely why explicit frames are discipline, not necessity, in this case.
exercise.solution:
-- (b) ranked (real SQLite / PostgreSQL)
SELECT role, avg_hours, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY avg_hours DESC) AS rnk
FROM (SELECT role, AVG(hours_studied) AS avg_hours FROM developers GROUP BY role) AS p;
-- running with explicit frame
SELECT role, avg_hours,
  SUM(avg_hours) OVER (ORDER BY avg_hours DESC ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW) AS running
FROM (SELECT role, AVG(hours_studied) AS avg_hours FROM developers GROUP BY role) AS p;
exercise.why: The exercise makes pipeline order tangible (windows over grouped output) and defaults visible (frame deletion changes nothing *here* — the dangerous lesson is that it changes everything *somewhere else*, which is why explicitness is the rule).

quiz.q: SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY role) vs SUM(x) OVER (PARTITION BY role ORDER BY x) — difference?
options: None — ORDER BY only sorts output
First: whole-partition total on every row; second: growing-prefix running total (ORDER BY flips the default frame)
quiz.explain: OVER's ORDER BY sequences peers and switches the default frame to running. Same function, different peer sets — the silent switch behind most window surprises.

quiz.q: Why must top-N-per-group filter ranks in an outer query?
options: Pipeline order: WHERE evaluates before windows exist — rank inside, filter outside
quiz.explain: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → windows → SELECT → ORDER BY. Same-level WHERE predates the window alias; the wrapper is structural, not stylistic.

quiz.q: You add ORDER BY inside OVER 'to sort the output'. What breaks?
options: Aggregates silently become running computations (default frame flips); output sorting belongs in the query's ORDER BY
quiz.explain: OVER's ORDER BY defines peer sequence for ranking/frames, not presentation. Display sorting is the query-level ORDER BY's job — confusing them converts totals into running totals.

quiz.q: When is an explicit frame unnecessary yet still recommended?
options: Never — omit it when defaults suffice
When the default already matches (e.g., growing prefix wanted): explicitness documents intent and immunizes against future edits that change defaults
quiz.explain: Explicit frames are discipline: today's correct default becomes tomorrow's bug when someone adds ORDER BY. Three words delete a bug class.

summary: Partition slices, order sequences (and flips defaults), frame bounds — three dials, pipeline position after grouping, explicit frames always. The model that makes every later lesson predictable.
